source_text: Chapter I introduces the equations of fluid mechanics and later models, recommends references [90, 66, 102, 127, 126, 123], and points to Appendix B for thermodynamics.
A fluid consists of many moving molecules. A statistical particle-interaction approach leads to kinetic theory and statistical mechanics and goes back to Maxwell.
When characteristic lengths are large compared with the mean free path, the fluid may be treated as a continuous medium and described by macroscopic density and velocity.

An elementary volume delta V contains mass delta m and many molecules; density and velocity are described by the displayed statistical ratios, essentially independently of the admissible choice of delta V.
Definition I.1.1 states that the continuous-medium description is valid when a nonnegative density field rho represents the mass of every fluid volume by Equation (I.1).

The integral representation requires volumes larger than the mean free path. Numerical orders of magnitude for gases and water are compared with rarefied high-altitude flow, where a microscopic description becomes necessary.
Common differential-operator notation and properties are reviewed in Appendix A.
Lagrangian coordinates follow a fluid particle or volume element, whereas Eulerian coordinates belong to a fixed experimental frame; the book uses the Eulerian description.
The flow is described by bijective maps phi_t on the initial fluid volume, with Omega_t containing exactly the molecules initially in Omega_0 and with no matter source or sink.
Definition I.1.2 names the transported family (Omega_t)_t a fluid element and calls the singleton case a fluid particle.
The position phi_t(x_0) and the map X(t,t_0,x_0) define the position and trajectory of a fluid particle.
The macroscopic velocity field is defined by the kinematic relations (I.2) and (I.3).
Remark I.1.1 states that a sufficiently smooth known velocity determines the position field through the characteristic equation (I.4).
The Eulerian description fixes X. The material derivative is defined in (I.5), and the following chain-rule calculation explains it.
